title_ar: شرح نخبة الفكر في مصطلح أهل الأثر الشريط الثالث
title_en: Commentary on Nukhbat al-Fikr on the terminology of the people of hadith — tape three
body_ar: عادم الضبط يسمى ضعيفا، والضعيف أنواع أخرى وخفيف الضبط يسمى صدوقا، فمثلا إذا وجدت إسنادا فوجدت في تراجمه فلان ثقة فلان ثقة فلان صدوق مثلا فستحكم على هذا الحديث أنه حسن لأن في رجاله واحد وصف بأنه صدوق معناه أن الضبط قد خف، لكن إذا وجدت الإسناد جميعا فلان ثقة فلان ثقة فلان ثقة وأثبت أنه سمع من فلان وأنه ثقة في كل ما حدث به أو ثقة في حديثه عن فلان فتحكم بالصحة وإذا وجدت فيه فلان مثلا ضعيف فستحكم بالضعف ولو كان الجميع موصوفا بالثقة إلا واحدا تحكم بالضعف، ولو كان أيضا جميعهم من الثقات إلا واحدا حكم بأنه صدوق لا يكون الحديث صحيحا بل يكون حسنا، إذن هذا الشرط هو الثاني من شروط الصحيح هو الضبط.
body_en: One who lacks precision (ḍabṭ) is called weak, and the weak has other kinds besides; and one whose precision is slight is called ṣadūq. So for example, if you find a chain of transmission and find in the biographical entries of its narrators "so-and-so, trustworthy; so-and-so, trustworthy; so-and-so, ṣadūq", for instance, you will judge of this hadith that it is good (ḥasan), because among its men is one described as ṣadūq, which means that the precision has become slight. But if you find the chain to be, throughout, "so-and-so, trustworthy; so-and-so, trustworthy; so-and-so, trustworthy", and it is established that he heard from so-and-so, and that he is trustworthy in everything he narrated, or trustworthy in his narration from so-and-so, then you judge it sound. And if you find in it "so-and-so, for example, weak", you will judge it weak: even if all of them were described as trustworthy but one, you judge it weak. And likewise, even if all of them were among the trustworthy but one who was judged to be ṣadūq, the hadith is not sound but good. So this condition is the second of the conditions of the sound report: it is precision (ḍabṭ).

flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY, and a different defect from the excerpt truncation found elsewhere in this range. This record is truncated at the BEGINNING, not only at the end: it opens mid-argument with no doxology, no naming of the tape and no statement of what is being discussed, unlike every other record in the series. A reader arriving at this page is given the tail of a definition of ḍabṭ with the first condition of a sound report, and the definition of ḍabṭ itself, missing. The full transcript is behind the .docx download in source_download_link.

flags.note: A grading of a narrator, not a description of character, and it is not in the project glossary. Rendering it as 'truthful' invites an English reader to take it as praise rather than as a rank that places a report below 'sound'. The whole passage turns on the rank, so option 0 keeps the Arabic. Thiqah has been rendered 'trustworthy' throughout for the same reason — as a rank. The glossary should be extended with both.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The date shown by the CMS is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on Ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani's Nukhbat al-Fikr, a short manual of hadith terminology. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 628–637 and the tape numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the tape number in the title, not by id, and even then a gap remains (see the note on the download filenames).

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text is the opening of a lecture and breaks off; the full transcript is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.
'Sound' and 'good' are used for ṣaḥīḥ and ḥasan as hadith gradings, per the glossary. Ṣaḥīḥ is not 'valid' here, since the subject is a report and not an act or a contract.

'Precision' renders ḍabṭ — a narrator's accuracy in retaining and reproducing what he heard. It is the second of the five conditions of a sound report and is not in the project glossary; it should be added.

The shifts between 'you will judge', 'you judge' and the impersonal 'it is judged' are in the Arabic, which moves between second person and third person; they have been followed rather than regularised.
